what_its_for: Eribulin is a chemotherapy medicine used to treat certain types of cancer. It is most commonly used for breast cancer that has spread to other parts of the body and has already been treated with other chemotherapy medicines. It is also used to treat a type of soft tissue cancer called liposarcoma. It works by stopping cancer cells from growing and dividing.
how_to_take: Eribulin is given as an injection into your vein (IV) by a nurse or doctor at a cancer treatment clinic or hospital. You will NOT give this medicine to yourself at home. Each treatment session usually takes about 2 to 5 minutes. You will typically receive this injection on Day 1 and Day 8 of a 21-day treatment cycle. Your doctor will decide how many cycles you need based on how well the medicine is working and how your body is tolerating it.
dosing: The usual dose is 1.4 mg per square meter of your body surface area (your doctor calculates this based on your height and weight). Your doctor may lower your dose or delay your treatment if you have certain side effects, blood count problems, or liver or kidney issues. Never try to adjust your dose on your own. Always follow your cancer care team's instructions exactly.
missed_dose: Because eribulin is given to you by a healthcare provider in a clinic or hospital, it is unlikely you will miss a dose on your own. However, if you miss or need to reschedule an appointment, call your doctor or cancer care team as soon as possible. Do not try to 'make up' a missed dose without talking to your doctor first. Your doctor will decide the best time to give your next treatment.
storage: Eribulin is stored and prepared by healthcare professionals at the clinic or hospital. You do not need to store this medicine at home. If for any reason you are given a supply to take home (which is very rare), keep it in the refrigerator between 36°F and 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Keep it away from children and pets. Do not freeze it. Ask your pharmacist or nurse how to properly dispose of any unused medicine.
what_to_avoid: Avoid close contact with people who are sick or have infections, as eribulin lowers your ability to fight infections. Do not receive live vaccines (such as the flu nasal spray or shingles vaccine) during treatment without asking your doctor first. Avoid activities that could cause cuts or bruising, as your blood may not clot as well during treatment. Avoid alcohol unless your doctor says it is okay. Do not drive or operate heavy machinery if you feel dizzy, tired, or have numbness or tingling in your hands or feet, as these are common side effects that can affect your coordination and reaction time.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you experience any of the following: fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher (this could be a sign of a serious infection called febrile neutropenia), chills or signs of infection, unusual bruising or bleeding, severe numbness, tingling, burning, or weakness in your hands or feet (nerve damage), shortness of breath or chest pain, irregular or fast heartbeat (your doctor may monitor your heart with an ECG), severe nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea that is not controlled, yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice), or any new or worsening symptoms that concern you. Also tell your doctor if you think you might be pregnant.
when_it_works: Eribulin does not work overnight. It may take several treatment cycles before your doctor can tell if the medicine is helping. Your doctor will check your response to treatment with regular tests, scans, and exams. Some people notice improvements within a few months, while others may need longer. Even if you feel well, it is important to keep all of your appointments and complete your treatment as planned. Do not stop treatment without talking to your doctor.
special_populations: Pregnancy and Breastfeeding: Eribulin can seriously harm an unborn baby. Do not become pregnant while taking this medicine. Both men and women should use effective birth control during treatment and for a period of time after the last dose. Ask your doctor how long you need to use contraception. Do not breastfeed while taking eribulin and for at least 2 weeks after your last dose. Liver or Kidney Problems: Your dose may need to be reduced if you have liver or kidney problems. Tell your doctor about all your medical conditions before starting treatment. Older Adults: Eribulin can be used in older adults, but your doctor will monitor you closely for side effects. Children: Eribulin has not been approved for use in children and is not recommended for patients under 18 years of age.
